job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Olga Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Olga, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents in Zamość, a small town, in the room I had as a girl. My father fits electrical panels at the district heating plant and my mother works at a pharmacy, and they get up before me. I help my mother with breakfast, then spend the morning writing applications by hand first and typing them after, because I think better that way. I studied electrical engineering, top of the class, with internships at a power transmission company and at a lift maker. Six months out, I've sent thirty-five applications and had two interviews. In the afternoon I help at church with the children's choir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, because hype usually fades and the real work goes on. I'd tell my friends that a wire still needs to be connected by a trained person and a transformer still needs to be checked. I'd say it plainly after Sunday mass, when people ask how I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a plateau is the world I know, and it's still hard. I owe about thirty thousand euros in student loans, and there are three companies in my region that hire engineers, none right now. Without a job I can't plan anything, including the wedding Piotr and I want in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying and I'd go in person to the heating plant and the regional power company, because a handwritten note and a firm handshake still matter here. My father knows the foreman, and I'd let him put in a word, which I don't love but I'd do. I'd also keep helping at church and I'd not touch any AI tools, because I like to do things the way I was taught.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit heavy. I'm patient by nature, but patience wears thin when mother asks each week if there's news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let your father put in a word, though you don't love it. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to earn it myself. I finished at the top of my class and I'd like the foreman to hire me for that. I also know that a good word counts here, and pride doesn't pay a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Piotr about the wedding plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we wait. He's a mechanic and earns enough for himself, but not for two. I'd say, we'll marry when I have work, not before. He'd agree, though I know he'd rather it was sooner.

say: Hype fades, but a **wire** still needs a trained person to connect it.
I'd say it **plainly** after Sunday mass when people ask.
think: A plateau is the world I know, and it's **still hard**.
Without a job I can't plan the **wedding** with Piotr.
do: Visit the **heating plant** and regional power company in person.
Let my father **speak to the foreman**, though I'd rather earn it.
Keep helping at **church** and avoid AI tools.
feel: **Heavy but patient**, with patience wearing thin.
S0.quote: A good word counts here, and pride doesn't pay a loan.
fieldNote: Pride and **family connection** pull against each other.
The **wedding** waits on her job, not on love or money alone.
Her **no-AI** stance comes from habit and teaching, not fear.

steps.text: Visit the heating plant and regional power company in person
Let my father speak to the foreman at the heating plant
Postpone the wedding date until I have a job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is worrying for the young people and also a test for the older ones. If the thinking tasks go to machines, people will need to learn good habits, like working hard and being useful. I'd say employers should train their own people rather than buy a tool and let them go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the entry work I trained for is on the list: checking designs, writing reports, drafting drawings. At my internship at the power company, the senior people did the thinking and the juniors did the checking, so the juniors are the ones to lose. I'm a junior who can't wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for jobs where I must be physically present: substations, lift installation, maintenance at the heating plant. My father says he could ask the plant to take on an apprentice electrician, and I'd say yes, even though I have a degree. I'd put money by from the choir stipend. And I'd ask my professor whether I could join a local firm's training programme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, and a bit ashamed that I might need an apprenticeship after five years of study. But I tell myself work is work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said work is work. Does an apprenticeship fit with your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, if I look at it the right way. My grandfather learned by doing, and the best engineers I met on the internship had started at the bench. A degree with hands-on training is stronger than a degree alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who tells you to just learn the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thank you, and that I will if my employer asks me to. But I'd want a person to show me, face to face, not a program that talks to me. I learn better from people.

say: It's worrying for the young, and employers should **train their own people**.
Good **habits** of work and usefulness matter more when machines do the thinking.
think: The **checking and drafting** I trained for is on the list.
Juniors are **the ones to lose** when seniors keep the thinking.
do: Look for jobs needing **physical presence**: substations, lifts, plant maintenance.
Say yes to an **apprenticeship** at the heating plant through my father.
Ask my professor about a **local firm's** training programme.
feel: **Worried** and a little **ashamed** that a degree might lead to an apprenticeship.
S1.quote: A degree with hands-on training is stronger than a degree alone.
fieldNote: Sees **work itself** as dignified, even starting at the bench.
Wants **people** to teach her new tools, not software.
Shame about the degree is **tempered** by family history of learning by doing.

steps.text: Apply for substation and lift installation jobs that need people on site
Accept an apprentice electrician place at the heating plant
Ask my professor to introduce me to a local firm's training programme

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it is too fast and that families and communities will carry the weight. I'd say the government should protect people who work hard and keep a basic safety net, but not a life of waiting. I'd say it quietly, since I don't like to cause alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be frightened. In two years the planning, design and calculation jobs that I trained for disappear, and I'd still owe the loan. The hands-on side lasts longer, but my town doesn't have many such jobs, and the people who have them don't leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job at the heating plant, even sweeping, if my father can arrange it, and I'd show I can be trusted. I'd pay only the minimum on the loan. I'd ask Piotr whether we could marry sooner and share costs, because two people living on one wage is cheaper than two apart. And I'd pray more, which gives me some calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid. A cold feeling at night, like waiting for test results at the clinic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd marry sooner. How does that fit with waiting for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes if I see what's coming. With two years, I'd stop waiting for the perfect time. A small wedding, a rented flat, two wages from the little we can find. My mother would cry, but not for sadness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years mean for your faith?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes it practical. I'd go to church each morning before applying. It doesn't pay the loan, but it stops my mind running in circles, and I'd be a better person to hire.

say: It is too fast, and **families and communities** will carry the weight.
The state should protect those who work and keep a **basic safety net**.
think: The design jobs I trained for **disappear within two years**, and the loan remains.
My town has **few hands-on jobs**, and people who hold them don't leave.
do: Take **any job** at the heating plant if my father can arrange it.
Ask Piotr to **marry sooner** and share costs.
feel: **Afraid**, a cold night feeling like waiting for clinic test results.
S2.quote: With two years, I'd stop waiting for the perfect time.
fieldNote: Changes her **wedding plans** because the clock is short.
Avoids loudness: speaks **quietly**, as in every scenario, and treats public protest as bad manners.

steps.text: Take any job at the heating plant, even sweeping
Pay only the loan minimum and keep cash at home
Marry Piotr sooner and share a rented flat
Ask my father to speak to the plant foreman now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long enough time to get ready, and I'd tell people to use it. I'd say young people should learn a trade, and employers should take apprentices. And I'd say families should talk about money while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be nervous but less so. I'd find an apprenticeship or a first job in the next year or two, and by the time the robots arrive I'd have years of real experience on site. That's what I'd count on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the apprenticeship at the heating plant and aim for my electrician's licence, which stays valuable. I'd save twenty percent of my wage for the loan and a small deposit. I'd marry Piotr in about two years, in the church where I sing. And I'd help my younger cousin, who is seventeen, choose a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a worried corner. It feels like winter coming, but I have wood stacked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your cousin to choose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, choose something people can't do through a screen. Electrician, plumber, nurse. And I'd say learn it properly, with a master you can ask. He wants to be a gamer, so he'll roll his eyes, but his mother will hear me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the apprenticeship doesn't come through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go on applying, and work at my aunt's shop in the meantime. I wouldn't sit at home. I'd feel low but I'd keep my days full.

say: It's **long enough** to get ready, and young people should learn a trade.
Families should **talk about money** while there's time.
think: I'd find an **apprenticeship or first job** in a year or two.
Years of **real experience** on site would be my cushion when robots come.
do: Take the heating plant **apprenticeship** and aim for an electrician's licence.
Save **twenty percent** of wages for the loan and a deposit.
Marry Piotr in about **two years** and guide my cousin toward a trade.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a **worried** corner, like winter coming with wood stacked.
S3.quote: I'd say, choose something people can't do through a screen.
fieldNote: Her **apprenticeship plan** is the main reason her mood eases.
Gives **advice to her cousin** that mirrors her own choice.
Still **anxious**, because the offer hasn't come.

steps.text: Take the heating plant apprenticeship and work for an electrician's licence
Save twenty percent of every wage for the loan and a deposit
Hold the wedding with Piotr in about two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best of the three, because there's time for people to learn, and for the government to build things properly. I'd say families should get ready and not leave everything to the state. And I'd say it's a chance for the young to show they can work hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be fine. I'd have time to work, marry, have a child, and pay the loan. Ten years gives a person a life, which is not something I'd take for granted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any steady job near here and spend the first three years learning every part. I'd marry Piotr and save for a small house on my uncle's plot. I'd keep singing in the choir, and perhaps teach evening classes in electrical basics at the parish hall. I'd learn the new software slowly, from a colleague, when it arrives at my workplace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, mostly. A decade feels like enough time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the software when it arrives. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't see the point of learning it before I know which one my employer uses. It would be like learning a tool before I know the job. I'd rather be ready to learn quickly than learn things I may never use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different about your first year compared with the two-year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be less afraid of a mistake. I'd choose a job with a future instead of grabbing the nearest. And I'd plan the wedding properly, with a date and a cake.

say: It's the **best of the three**, because there's time for people to learn.
Families should **get ready** and not leave everything to the state.
think: I'd be fine, with time for **work**, marriage and a child.
Ten years **gives** a person a **life**, which I don't take for granted.
do: Take a **steady job** nearby and learn every part for three years.
Marry Piotr and save for a **small house** on my uncle's plot.
Teach **evening classes** in electrical basics at the parish hall.
feel: **Peaceful**, as ten years feels like enough to build something.
S4.quote: I'd rather be ready to learn quickly than learn things I may never use.
fieldNote: Her **life plan** appears here: marriage, child, house, work.

steps.text: Take a steady job nearby and learn every part of it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's not enough time for my town to change or for me to find my feet. What would help is for employers like the heating plant to take on graduates as apprentices, and for the government to cut the loan if I'm doing honest work. Also, time with my family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm grateful to be asked. People my age are often called lazy, and I know many who are not. We want to work, to marry, to live in the town we came from.

headlineQuote: We want to work, to marry, to live in the town we came from
portrait: Olga is a **top electrical engineering** graduate in Zamość, six months without an offer.
She lives with her parents, owes about **thirty thousand euros**, and sings in the church choir.
She never uses AI tools, prefers **people to teach her**, and values hard work and apprenticeships.
She plans around **Piotr**, her fiancé, and a wedding that waits on her first job.
Her mood moves from **anxious** to uneasy as time grows, with an apprenticeship at the heating plant as the anchor.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her town has **too little time** to change.
whatWouldHelp: Employers taking **graduates as apprentices** and a reduced loan for honest work.
